meta.title: Who really said "Humor Can Be Dissected, as a Frog Can, But the Thing Dies in the Process"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine E. B. White. Verified on page xvii of the 1941 preface to A Subtreasury of American Humor — not Mark Twain, who got the credit in the 1980s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Humor Can Be Dissected, as a Frog Can, But the Thing Dies in the Process'?
meta.ogDescription: Confirmed in the 1941 book: E. B. White's preface to A Subtreasury of American Humor, p. xvii. The Mark Twain version is a later misattribution.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1899–1985 · essayist and contributing editor, The New Yorker
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. The sentence opens a paragraph in the Preface to A Subtreasury of American Humor (Coward-McCann, 1941), page xvii — the anthology E. B. White edited with his wife, Katharine S. White. The preface is signed “E. B. W.” and written in the first person singular, but the book is copyright to both Whites, and Quote Investigator credits the pair jointly ↗ because the same text also ran under both bylines in The Saturday Review of Literature on 18 October 1941. The full sentence ends “…and the innards are discouraging to any but the pure scientific mind.”

source.excerpt: Analysts have had their go at humor, and I have read some of this interpretative literature, but without being greatly instructed. Humor can be dissected, as a frog can, but the thing dies in the process and the innards are discouraging to any but the pure scientific mind.
trail: 1941 — The sentence appears in the Preface to A Subtreasury of American Humor, page xvii, in the paragraph beginning “Analysts have had their go at humor.” The scanned first edition carries it verbatim ↗.
18 October 1941 — The same text runs in The Saturday Review of Literature as “The Preaching Humorist,” bylined E. B. White and Katharine S. White, page 16. WIST Quotations records that citation ↗.
1960 and 1976 — André Maurois and then Marty Feldman use their own versions of the frog simile in print, spreading it without the Whites’ name. Quote Investigator dates and quotes both ↗.
1985 onward — American newspapers begin crediting reworded versions to Mark Twain, and one column re-words White himself. QI finds no substantive evidence for the Twain link ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned 1941 Coward-McCann edition. Note the book’s reading, “pure scientific mind”; the Saturday Review printing of the same text has “purely.” Both wordings are authentic to 1941.

author.name: E. B. White
author.heading: Who was E. B. White?
author.metaLine: 1899–1985 · New Yorker essayist and author of Charlotte’s Web
author.bio: Elwyn Brooks White (11 July 1899 – 1 October 1985) joined The New Yorker in 1927 and became, in the magazine’s own reckoning, its most important contributor — the voice behind decades of essays and unsigned “Notes and Comment” paragraphs. He is best known now for Charlotte’s Web (1952) and Stuart Little (1945), and for revising The Elements of Style. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1963 and a Pulitzer Prize special citation in 1978. The 1941 humor anthology that carries this sentence was assembled with his wife, Katharine S. White (1892–1977), The New Yorker’s fiction editor from 1925 to 1960.

misattribution.heading: Who it isn’t, and which wording isn’t his
misattribution.intro: The thought is White’s and the sentence is real, but almost none of the versions circulating today are the one he wrote — and the name attached is often not his at all.

items.why: The commonest credit online, and unsupported. Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Twain used the simile ↗; the earliest Twain ascription it documents is a Sacramento Bee feature of 29 March 1985, followed by a 1987 Los Angeles Times epigraph and a 2013 Publishers Weekly review.

items.scope: “Analyzing wit and humor is like dissecting a frog…”
items.why: Maurois genuinely used the image — in a 1960 talk at NYU’s French cultural centre, reported by columnist Leonard Lyons on 7 December 1960 — but QI concludes he was a populariser, not the originator ↗.

items.scope: “You can learn the parts and label them, but you kill the frog…”
items.why: Feldman used his own version to deflect an interviewer in a New York Times profile of 23 July 1976. QI places it downstream of the 1941 text ↗.

items.scope: “Analyzing humor is like dissecting a frog. Few people are interested and the frog dies of it.”
items.who: E. B. White — but not in these words
items.why: Right author, wrong sentence. Wikiquote notes it “may actually be a paraphrased version” of the 1941 line ↗, and QI traces this exact phrasing to a San Francisco Chronicle column of 25 October 1985 ↗ that put it in White’s mouth.

misattribution.truthLine: What White actually wrote, on page xvii of the 1941 preface: “Humor can be dissected, as a frog can, but the thing dies in the process and the innards are discouraging to any but the pure scientific mind.” You can read it in the scanned first edition ↗.

context.heading: Why the frog keeps getting cut open
lead: White wrote the sentence as a shrug, not a manifesto. It sits near the end of a rambling, deliberately unserious preface in which he explains why Harry Leon Wilson and Thoreau are missing from the anthology, apologises for including his own pieces (“an unsavory episode upon which I shall not dwell”), and admits that he and his wife assembled much of the book by pulling bound volumes of The New Yorker off a shelf before bed. The frog arrives in a single paragraph about academic humor theory: he had read the interpretative literature, he says, “without being greatly instructed.”

The line escaped the book almost immediately and then drifted off its author. By 1960 the French novelist André Maurois was using the simile in a New York lecture; by 1976 Marty Feldman was using it to fend off an interviewer; and by 1985 American newspapers had started handing it to Mark Twain, which is where most of today’s internet versions come from. Quote Investigator traces that whole chain ↗ and finds no substantive evidence Twain ever wrote anything like it.
detailsBody: The magazine text and the book text differ by one letter’s worth of grammar. The Saturday Review of Literature version reads “any but the purely scientific mind”; the book’s preface reads “any but the pure scientific mind.” Quote Investigator flags the difference in its bibliographic note ↗, and the 1941 book scan confirms the “pure” reading. Both are E. B. White; neither is wrong to quote.

A modified form of the 1941 preface was later collected as an essay under the title “Some Remarks on Humor,” which is how the piece is usually cited today — and how it is reprinted by Narrative Magazine ↗, carrying the “pure scientific mind” wording. In the 1941 volume itself the section is headed simply “Preface.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes E. B. White and Katharine S. White originated the line in 1941, cites The Saturday Review of Literature of 18 October 1941 ("The Preaching Humorist", p. 16) and A Subtreasury of American Humor (Coward-McCann, 1941, Preface, p. xvii, verified on paper), notes the Preface reads "pure" where the magazine reads "purely", documents Maurois (7 Dec 1960, Leonard Lyons), Feldman (NYT, 23 July 1976), and Mark Twain ascriptions from the Sacramento Bee of 29 March 1985, the Los Angeles Times of 20 Dec 1987 and Publishers Weekly in 2013, plus a San Francisco Chronicle column of 25 Oct 1985 giving White the paraphrase "Analyzing humor is like dissecting a frog. Few people are interested. And the frog dies of it." — and finds no substantive evidence for Twain.

The scanned 1941 Coward-McCann first edition of A Subtreasury of American Humor contains, in the Preface at page xvii, "Analysts have had their go at humor, and I have read some of this interpretative literature, but without being greatly instructed. Humor can be dissected, as a frog can, but the thing dies in the process and the innards are discouraging to any but the pure scientific mind." The preface is signed "E. B. W." and the copyright page reads "Copyright, 1941, by E. B. White and Katharine S. White."

Wikiquote gives the quotation as "Humor can be dissected, as a frog can, but the thing dies in the process and the innards are discouraging to any but the pure scientific mind," sources it to "Some Remarks on Humor," preface to A Subtreasury of American Humor (1941), and notes that the similar "Analyzing humor is like dissecting a frog. Few people are interested and the frog dies of it" may be a paraphrased version.

WIST Quotations cites the line to "The Preaching Humorist," The Saturday Review of Literature (18 October 1941), with Katharine White co-credited, and notes the Mark Twain and André Maurois misattributions.
Narrative Magazine reprints the essay under the title "Some Remarks on Humor" by E. B. White, containing the sentence with the wording "pure scientific mind."
A Subtreasury of American Humor was published by Coward-McCann, Inc. in 1941 and edited by E. B. White and Katharine White.

E. B. White (Elwyn Brooks White) lived 11 July 1899 – 1 October 1985, joined The New Yorker staff in 1927, wrote Stuart Little (1945) and Charlotte's Web (1952), received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1963 and a Pulitzer Prize special citation in 1978, and co-edited A Subtreasury of American Humor (1941) with Katharine S. White.
Katharine Sergeant Angell White lived 17 September 1892 – 20 July 1977 and was fiction editor of The New Yorker from 1925 to 1960.
